title: Godot + AI has conquered retro romhacking and modding
author: WorkAccountObv
selftext:
So, I know the title is a bit sensationalist but this was the first time since starting to use AI I have been genuinely amazed at what I was able to build in a short amount of time. 

This project is a complete rom editing tool for the original Super Mario Kart. 

Modify tracks, AI, sprites, physics etc and then you can export the rom to play on a real SNES. You simply provide the original ROM as no assets are kept or stored by the editor itself.

Impressive right? Well, the actual impressive part is the copy of the game running in the editor. This is a 1:1 recreation of SMK running natively in GDScript with some CPP helpers (sound engine being the main one). The way this was accomplished was by Astra finding a disassembly of the game on the web and then running its own disassembler to fill in the gaps on anything that was missing or misunderstood. By being a near 1:1 recreation in a modern engine, you can just simply apply modern game dev techniques ontop to modify the new copy. Ofcourse I can't export this to play on a real SNES but I now have a near cycle accurate port I can run anywhere GODOT can run. 

Modding is super easy, want the walls raised? One click, want the Kart replaced? One click. Want to copy the physics and build on them for another project? Cake. 

I was able to build this tool start to finish over 4 days of prompting with very minimal input and guidance. Astra even modified the Goomba sprite with asesprite directly and created the replacement logo on the title screen and it admitedly looks terrible but just the fact it could attempt it directly in a tool like asesprite is.... wild?

If you have any questions let me know!

I never ran into any safeguards. I’m also not storing or distributing any of the copyrighted assets.

I would argue porting the code may fall under it but it’s the disassembly of the code it’s using as reference not the original code?

comments.body:
This looks awesome.

I’ve been doing something similar with Phantasy Star IV on the Genesis. I was using 5.6 Sol and had it running in Godot. It wasn’t perfect yet but now that Astra is out and seeing your success, I may dig back into it.

replies.author: Economy_Drama_8757
replies.body: Firstly, Phantasy Star IV is one of my favorite games of all time... so like you I had the idea of porting/modernizing it. My first attempt was bit grand but I had attempted disassemble it so I could convert the whole game to a modern HD-2D vibe. It was going well on the programmatic side of things... unfortunately there was ton of hand holding when it came to upscaling the sprites so I had to pause on it. This was before astra though so I might check out what it's capable of.

replies.author: cerrakin
replies.body: Yes. Sol did a good job of getting it all extracted and into data we could use in Godot. I was doing a Rust backend and putting all the adjustable data in json files for easy editing and modification later. The issue I kept running into is that just things like battle screens, cutscenes, etc were engineered in a way that unless I had Sol looking at it side by side with an emulator, it had no clue how some of it was done. So it was a ton of handholding and almost scene by scene in some areas. I’m guessing it’d be easier now with Astra.

replies.author: WorkAccountObv
replies.body: There are plenty of tools out there to disassemble roms, in most cases it’s one click. The hard part is comparing, labeling data and functions etc. If a LLM has an emulator to compare the disassembled data to it becomes trivial for it to document it and work with it.

replies.author: WorkAccountObv
replies.body:
Correct. It did determine for sound and some other CPU quirks it should use cpp but it just built native extensions for Godot. 95% of the logic is in gdscript. 

To replicate the SNES graphics mode7 it chose to just build it in a shader.

replies.author: SyrysSylynys
replies.body: I've been using ChatGPT 5.6 Sol extensively for doing this kind of thing with old (1982 - 1985 era) Commodore 64 games. You can literally just upload a D64 disk image and it'll figure everything out on its own, up to and including writing itself a small 6502 emulator to do dynamic code analysis if static analysis fails. It doesn't matter if it's BASIC, machine language, or a combination. Heck, it was even able to determine that one program I gave it was written in an ancient version of Forth, which I didn't even know was a thing on the C64. It absolutely blows my mind that it's this capable with such "ancient" technology.

replies.author: WorkAccountObv

You’ll have to Google to see if a particular game is already disassembled or you can literally prompt the LLm now to disassemble and reverse engineer a provided rom. 

Just instruct codex to edit the pixel art directly with asesprite instead of image gen and it will do so if it’s installed. It doe it by writing scripts which asesprite uses to generate assets, not by controlling the paint tool etc.

comments.author: Lacutis
comments.body:
Yeah, I've been working on a complete recreation of an old TBS game "Birth of the Federation". I'm about 3-4 days in and have a large portion of the game recreated at this point. I've never done a reverse engineering project but its been really interesting watching how Astra approaches it, uses disassembly tools, and plans out how it works through the executable. 

It really quickly got to a point where it could load a save file, edit values within it, and render the models within the packed files shipped with the game. The rest of the time has been around meticulously recreating the AI (including bugs) and getting a full turn cycle working. I'm also using Godot for the rendering engine, but writing the core engine of the game in C#.

Really interesting stuff.
